Last time every response ran from stimulus to receptor to command centre to effector, and now you'll look at the two ways the message actually gets sent.

## Engage: how does insulin get there?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Students who think all control runs through nerves, or that hormones travel along nerves, pick those options; the blood as the carrier is the idea to build."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "After a meal, your pancreas releases insulin, which tells your liver to store glucose. How does the insulin get from the pancreas to the liver?"
  options: ["In the blood", "Along a nerve", "It is made in the liver", "Through the stomach"]
  actual: "In the blood. Insulin is a hormone: a chemical message released by a gland into the blood, which carries it everywhere; only target organs, such as the liver, respond."
```

## Explore: two pathways

```step
stage: run
insight: "Sending a nervous and a hormonal response through the same five boxes, then building four pathways, shows one model with two messengers."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#pathway", height: 640 }
tasks:
  - starter: "boards.yml#pathway"
    check: { type: board, text: "Send both stimuli through the pathway. What is different about the command centre?", when: "n >= 2" }
  - starter: "boards.yml#build"
    check: { type: board, text: "Build all four pathways: two nervous, two hormonal.", when: "c >= 4" }
    hint: ["For the hormone pathways, ask what releases the hormone and which of the five boxes that part belongs in.", "When the signal stops, the message under the boxes names the part that doesn't fit, so change just that one, and remember the effector is the organ that ends up doing something different."]
```

### Two stimuli

Click a stimulus to send it through the five boxes.

### Build them

Choose the receptor, command centre and effector for each. Glands are command centres too: they release hormones.

## Explain: comparing the two systems

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Sorting by signal, speed, duration and reach, then naming glands and target organs, gives students the comparison framework the next lesson uses."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "Nervous system or endocrine (hormone) system?"
      options: ["Nervous", "Endocrine"]
      items:
        - ["Electrical signals along nerves", "Nervous"]
        - ["Chemical messages carried in the blood", "Endocrine"]
        - ["Very fast: a fraction of a second", "Nervous"]
        - ["Slower: seconds to hours", "Endocrine"]
        - ["Short-lived: stops when the signal stops", "Nervous"]
        - ["Lasts longer: until the hormone is broken down", "Endocrine"]
        - ["Goes to one precise place", "Nervous"]
        - ["Reaches the whole body; only target organs respond", "Endocrine", "Every cell gets the insulin; only cells with the right receptors respond."]
    hint: ["For each one, picture the two pathways you sent through the board, pulling your hand off the hot pan and bringing blood glucose down after a meal, and ask which one it sounds like.", "Think about how the message gets from the command centre to the effector in each, because that decides how fast it is, how long it lasts and where it can go."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "In a hormonal pathway, what is the command centre?"
      options: ["A gland, such as the pancreas, which releases the hormone", "The blood", "The target organ"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "The blood carries the message; it doesn't decide anything.", "The target organ is the effector."]
      explain: "Glands (pancreas, adrenal glands, pituitary) act as command centres: they detect or are told of a change and release a hormone."
    hint: ["Ask which of these actually decides to send a message, and which ones just carry it or act on it.", "In the hot pan the spinal cord sent the message along nerves, so ask what does that same job when the message is a hormone."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Why do electrical signals reach their effector faster than hormones?"
      options: ["They travel along nerves directly to one place; hormones drift around the body in the blood", "Electricity is stronger than chemicals", "Hormones have further to go because glands are far away"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Strength isn't the point; the route is.", "Distance matters less than how the message travels."]
      explain: "Nerve signals travel at up to about 100 m/s along a wired route. Hormones go wherever the blood goes, which takes about a minute for one lap of the body, and then must build up."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A fright makes you jump (nerves) and your heart keep pounding for minutes (adrenaline). Why use both?"
      options: ["Nerves give the instant reaction; the hormone keeps the whole body ready for longer", "The nerves stop working after a fright", "Adrenaline is a nerve signal"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Both systems work together.", "Adrenaline is a hormone, released by the adrenal glands into the blood."]
      explain: "Fast and short, plus slow and lasting: many responses use both systems."
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I can describe how the nervous and endocrine systems each carry a message, and compare their speed and how long they last." }
```

  - check:
      type: question
      q: "On a hot day with little to drink, the pituitary gland releases ADH, and the kidneys keep more water. Which is the effector?"
      options: ["The kidneys", "The pituitary gland", "ADH"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "The pituitary is the command centre: it releases the hormone.", "ADH is the messenger, not the effector."]
      explain: "Gland (command centre) → hormone in the blood (messenger) → kidneys (effector) → less water lost (response)."

## Evaluate: look back

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I compared my prediction about how insulin travels with the pathways I built." }
```

Write one sentence: "At first I thought… Now I think… because…"

**Revision summary**

- Both systems follow stimulus → receptor → command centre → effector → response.
- **Nervous system**: electrical signals along nerves, from the brain or spinal cord. Very fast, short-lived, to one place.
- **Endocrine system**: hormones released by **glands** (pancreas, adrenal glands, pituitary) into the blood. Slower, longer-lasting, reaching target organs anywhere.
- Many responses use both (a fright: a jump from nerves, a pounding heart from adrenaline).

```teacher
summary: Students describe how the nervous and endocrine systems each run the
  stimulus–receptor–command centre–effector pathway, and compare their signals,
  speed, duration and reach (AC9S9U01, node 3).
time: 25
timing: Engage and Explore 9 min · Explain 10 min · Evaluate 3 min · Typical
  adds 3 min, Wider about 3 min
goals:
  - I can explain how a nerve signal and a hormone each carry a message.
  - I can compare how fast each is and how long it lasts.
  - I can name glands as command centres and target organs as effectors.
before: >
  A concept tutorial for introducing or revising the idea. Set the width with
  `?width=minimum`, `typical` (default) or `wider`. It sits between Who decides?
  (the pathway, node 2) and Nerve or hormone? (comparing the systems in context,
  node 4), which uses the race board in more depth.


  Not a hinge node, but students often think every response runs through nerves,
  or that hormones travel along nerves. The prediction tests the second.


  Board notes: the pathways are simplified to five boxes. In the glucose pathway
  the pancreas both detects the change and releases insulin; in the fright
  pathway the brain triggers the adrenal glands by a nerve. The race graph is a
  sketch of the timescales, not measured data.
running:
  - "Engage: tally the predictions. 'Along a nerve' is the misconception to come
    back to."
  - "Explore: ask what kind of thing sat in the command centre box for each
    pathway."
  - "Explain: the sort is the success criterion; the 'why faster' question is
    the reason."
  - "In your own words: the two five-box pathways with the messenger labelled
    are the evidence."
struggle: Placing a gland in the pathway. When a student is stuck on the build
  board, ask 'what releases the hormone?' and let them find that it is the
  command centre.
stuck:
  - see: A student says hormones travel along nerves.
    ask: How does a medicine injected in your arm reach your whole body?
    fix: In the blood. Hormones are carried the same way.
  - see: A student thinks the blood is the command centre.
    ask: Does the blood decide anything, or just carry things?
    fix: It only carries. The gland that releases the hormone is the command centre.
  - see: A student thinks hormones affect every organ.
    ask: If insulin reaches your toes, why don't your toes store glucose like the
      liver?
    fix: Only target organs, with the right receptors, respond. The hormone reaches
      everywhere; the response doesn't.
stretch: Type 1 diabetes means the pancreas makes too little insulin. Which part
  of the pathway fails, and what happens to blood glucose after a meal? (The
  command centre's message is missing; glucose stays high.)
support: "Give a two-row table: Nervous | Endocrine, with columns Signal,
  Travels by, Speed, Lasts."
leads: >
  Next: Which system runs it? (node 4), then feedback (node 5).


  In class: reaction-time ruler drop (nerves) beside a discussion of how long a
  blush or a fright lasts (hormones); a map of the major glands.
exit:
  q: Give one difference between how a nerve signal and a hormone travel, and one
    difference in how long their effects last.
  a: Nerve signals are electrical, along nerves; hormones are chemicals in the
    blood. Nerve effects are brief; hormone effects last longer.
explain: >
  Both systems run stimulus → receptor → command centre → effector → response.
  The **nervous system** sends electrical signals along nerves: very fast,
  brief, to one place.


  The **endocrine system** uses **glands** that release **hormones** into the
  blood: slower, longer-lasting, reaching target organs anywhere. Many responses
  use both.
```
